documents.title: Artificial Intelligence in Education
documents.summary: The Academic Integrity Office hub on AI in education explains why AI literacy matters, defines it, and gives instructors a Canvas module and links to guides, events and consultations. It sets no use rule.
documents.stance_why: The page sets no rule on AI use; it says "Teaching, learning and assessments all need to change" and offers AI-literacy resources and guides for instructors, leaving policy to instructors ("Crafting Your GenAI Course Policy").

units.why: The page says "Teaching, learning and assessments all need to change" in response to LLMs, a general call to redesign teaching and assessment, so it is a P35 (redesign around AI) statement; it is a recommendation, not a rule, hence should/neutral.
units.anchor: Teaching, learning and assessments all need to change.
units.fit_note: Generic claim that teaching and assessment must change; no concrete redesign is specified.

units.why: The page lists what GenAI can do: "They can replace and augment human thinking" and "hinder and accelerate learning". It names both benefits and harms without making a rule, so it is a P87 benefits statement (the closest type; it is two-sided).
units.anchor: They can replace and augment human thinking.
units.frag_start: GenAI tools present both challenges and
units.fit_note: Two-sided: names harms (replace thinking, hinder learning) as well as benefits.

units.why: "Although there is not yet campus-sponsored AI Literacy training, you can help educate students" tells instructors to educate students in AI literacy themselves; this is AI-literacy provision (P70), and the quote also records that no campus training exists.
units.anchor: there is not yet campus-sponsored AI Literacy training, you can help educate students.
units.frag_end: ethically and responsibly for your course(s).
units.fit_note: States that no campus-sponsored AI literacy training exists and puts the task on instructors.

units.why: The page says the Canvas module "is meant as a resource to support instructors to introduce students to fundamental AI competencies", which is an institution-provided AI-literacy module for students (P70), not a rule.
units.anchor: to support instructors to introduce students to fundamental AI competencies
units.frag_start: The Critical AI Literacy Canvas Module

units.why: The passage says "Instructors may falsely believe that so-called AI detectors are valid and accurate", i.e. detectors are not reliable and should not be used to catch students; this is P39 (do not rely on detectors) stated as a warning.
units.anchor: so-called "AI detectors" are valid and accurate

units.why: The sentence about "the AI summary when you do a Google search" and Grammarly extends the scope of AI to tools "working behind the scenes", so it defines what counts as AI use (P61); it is a definitional/awareness statement.
units.anchor: Other AI tools are working behind the scenes
units.frag_start: Other AI tools are working behind
units.fit_note: Makes the point that everyday tools (Grammarly, search summaries) embed AI; it defines scope loosely rather than setting a definition.

units.why: "AI literacy is the ability to identify if, when, where, and why to use GenAI tools" is a definition of the term the university uses to frame its guidance, so P61 and informs.
units.anchor: AI literacy is the ability to identify if, when, where, and why to use GenAI
units.frag_start: AI literacy is the ability to
units.fit_note: Defines AI literacy, not AI itself.

units.why: "Critical evaluation of AI-generated content: Assessing AI outputs, understanding their origins, potential biases, and limitations" is a listed component of AI literacy that asks users to evaluate AI output, matching P31 (verify output), though framed as a competency.
units.anchor: Critical evaluation of AI-generated content: Assessing AI outputs
units.fit_note: Framed as an AI-literacy competency rather than a duty to verify.

units.why: "Ethical reasoning and risk awareness: Exploring moral implications of AI use, including privacy, fairness, and accountability" names ethical, privacy and bias concerns as part of AI literacy, which is P53.
units.anchor: Ethical reasoning and risk awareness: Exploring moral implications of AI use

units.why: "Adaptation and continuous learning: Staying informed about AI advancements" lists staying informed about AI as a component of AI literacy, matching P102.
units.anchor: Adaptation and continuous learning: Staying informed about AI advancements

units.why: "It's crucial to note that AI literacy is not about promoting AI use" states the purpose and principle of the university's literacy effort, so it is a framework/principle statement (P56) and neutral on stance.
units.anchor: AI literacy is not about promoting AI use.
units.frag_start: It's crucial to note that AI
units.frag_end: where human judgment and skills are irreplaceable.

units.why: "Create a Q&A discussion forum to encourage ongoing dialogue" is an instruction to instructors to keep discussing GenAI with students beyond announcing a rule; P66 (explain and discuss AI rules with students) fits.
units.anchor: Create a Q&A discussion forum to encourage ongoing dialogue

units.why: "Announce the module's availability using our sample announcement template" has instructors tell students about the AI-literacy Canvas module; the module is AI-literacy training (P70) and the announcement is communication, so P70 is the best home.
units.anchor: Announce the module's availability using our

units.why: "Engaged Teaching Hubs AI Literacy for Faculty Coffee Chats" lists a faculty-community offering about AI literacy, which is support for faculty learning about AI (P63).
units.anchor: Engaged Teaching Hubs AI Literacy for Faculty Coffee Chats

units.why: "Request a GenAI in Education Presentation, Workshop, or Consultation with Dr. Bertram Gallant" offers instructors workshops and consultations, i.e. faculty support (P63).

units.frag_start: Request a GenAI in Education Presentation

units.why: The resource list includes "Discussing GenAI with Your Students" and "Crafting Your GenAI Course Policy" as guide sections; the first is about talking to students about AI, so P66.
units.anchor: Discussing GenAI with Your Students
units.fit_note: Only a section title in a linked guide; the content is not in the fetched text.

units.why: "The Library's GenAI and Academic Integrity Guide" is listed under student resources, pointing students to a library guide as additional help, so P72.

documents.title: Top 10 Tips for Instructors
documents.summary: Ten integrity tips for instructors, mostly about building belonging, redesigning assessments, reminders, monitoring, evaluation and reporting. AI appears in the expectations tip, assessment redesign ideas and sample statement.
documents.stance_why: The tips set no AI stance of their own; they tell instructors to "Make Standards and Expectations Absolutely Clear" and craft their own "GenAI & AI Policy", while giving sample wording that bans tools doing students' work.

units.why: "it will help you build community and garner student buy-in if you do it with your students" recommends that instructors create the class statement of values or code of ethics together with students, which is P67.
units.anchor: build community and garner student buy-in if you do it with your students
units.frag_start: Sure, you could just tell them
units.fit_note: About integrity values in general, not only AI.

units.why: "must be aligned (and certainly not contradict) the university's Academic Integrity Policy" requires course statements to be consistent with the campus policy, so P77.
units.anchor: must be aligned (and certainly not contradict) the university's

units.why: "make sure to connect it to learning and/or evaluation" tells instructors to give students the reason behind non-negotiable rules; this is explaining the rules (P66).
units.anchor: make sure to connect it to learning and/or evaluation!
units.frag_start: Be clear on what is non-negotiable

units.why: "everyone is accountable for reporting violations of the code or values" makes the class community responsible for reporting violations, which is a duty to report misconduct (P71, nearest type).
units.anchor: everyone is accountable for reporting violations of the code or values
units.frag_start: Make sure they understand that once
units.fit_note: Applies to the class statement/code of ethics, not specifically to AI.

units.why: "Ensure that the learning objectives for the course are clearly stated, and each activity, assignment and exam are connected back" ties assessment to learning objectives, which matches P83.
units.anchor: Ensure that the learning objectives for the course are clearly stated
units.fit_note: Presented as an anti-cheating mastery design, not specifically about deciding AI use.

units.why: "Provide students some choice and control over the assessments" is advice to reduce the pressures behind cheating by giving choice, so P99.
units.anchor: Provide students some choice and control over the assessments.

units.why: "Provide multiple attempts at several low/no-stakes assessments" lowers stakes, a way to ease pressure to cheat (P99).
units.anchor: Provide multiple attempts at several low/
units.frag_start: Provide multiple attempts at several low/

units.why: "effective for combating cheating behaviors" is the stated reason for building belonging; connecting with students is a prevention measure, so P99.

units.why: "Given the advancements in artificial intelligence, be exceptionally clear!" tells instructors to state expectations about AI use and tools; the closest type is P09 (state AI expectations), though it is not tied to a syllabus.
units.anchor: Given the advancements in artificial intelligence, be exceptionally clear!
units.fit_note: Does not say the statement must be in the syllabus; it says expectations about AI must be clear.

units.why: The sample wording says "does not mean that you can get ... artificial intelligence to answer the exam questions for you", so open-book exams do not allow AI to answer questions; this is P22 (no AI on exams) in a suggested instructor phrase.
units.anchor: or artificial intelligence to answer the exam questions for
units.fit_note: Concerns open-book exams and is suggested wording for instructors, not a campus rule.

units.why: The sample statement says "Stay away from sites and tools (e.g., Chegg, Coursehero, ChatGPT, CoPilot) that will do your work for you", which bans having tools do the student's work (P19), as wording instructors may adopt.
units.anchor: Stay away from sites and tools (e.g., Chegg, Coursehero, ChatGPT, CoPilot)
units.frag_start: Stay away from sites and tools
units.fit_note: Suggested wording for instructors, not a campus rule.

units.why: The sample says such actions "result in an academic integrity violation and a report to the Academic Integrity Office", classifying tool-done work as misconduct (P36).
units.anchor: result in an academic integrity violation and a report to the Academic Integrity Office

units.why: "will undermine honesty and fairness, violate the trust of me and your peers" gives fairness and honesty as the reason for the AI limit, matching P95.
